confirmed.title: The ssh noticer starts stopped WSL distros: it picks distros from the cached running flag and runs wsl.exe -d <distro> in each
confirmed.scenario: Setup: WSL is on, and Ember read the facts while Ubuntu was running (at startup, refreshWsl sets wslFacts.distros[Ubuntu].running = true). The user closes their WSL tab and Ubuntu stops. With no WSLg window on screen, nothing reads the running set again: the router returns before facts() and the picker isn't opened, so wslFacts keeps running:true indefinitely. The user then runs `ssh deploy@build-01` in Windows Terminal. Because the title looks like ssh, noticer.check() runs. The wsl() closure (runtime.ts:943-947) passes distros:["Ubuntu"] from the stale flag, and userSshProcessesWith (notice-ssh.ts:316-321) runs `wsl.exe -d Ubuntu --exec /bin/sh -s`, which boots Ubuntu. Nothing checks runningNow(), and the probe is not under the job host. It happens again on every later check (title changes at least 10 s apart), each time after WSL has idled the distro back down. I reproduced it with the targets-runtime rig: wsl.runningNow() returned an empty set, the noticer still passed {wsl:{distros:["Ubuntu"]}}, and the real reader spawned ["C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe","-d","Ubuntu","--exec","/bin/sh","-s"]. This is a distro started by Ember without the user asking.
confirmed.fix: Choose the distros from an uncached read (await wsl.runningNow()) right before reading, or run the reader through WslRunner.runScript without mayBoot, which re-checks runningNow() and runs under the job host. Do not use wslFacts.running for anything that spawns wsl.exe.

votes.reason:
I could not refute it. I read the code and reproduced the scenario.

**Code path**
- The noticer's wsl() closure at /home/user/wt/sw-review/app/main/targets/runtime.ts:943-947 picks distros from the runtime's cached copy, `wslFacts.distros[].running`. It never calls `runningNow()`, or even `isRunning()`, which would at least start a background re-read.
- createNoticer.check() in /home/user/wt/sw-review/app/main/targets/offer.ts:86-89 passes that list unchanged to `userSshProcesses`.
- `userSshProcessesWith` in /home/user/wt/sw-review/app/main/remote/notice-ssh.ts:316-321 runs `[exe, "-d", distro, "--exec", "/bin/sh", "-s"]` through a plain execFile. That is not the job host and not `WslRunner.runScript`, which is the call that re-checks `runningNow()` unless `mayBoot`. `wsl.exe -d <distro>` starts a stopped distro (and the VM if needed). That is standard WSL behaviour, not something to verify.

**Why the flag stays stale**
`wslFacts` changes only through `wsl.onChange`. In /home/user/wt/sw-review/app/main/wsl/service.ts that fires only when `facts()`, `runningNow()` or `isRunning()` is called; nothing re-reads on a timer. The callers I found:
- the router's look(), which returns before `facts()` when no WSLg RAIL window is on screen (router.ts:307);
- the router's tick, which only runs while a helper sidecar exists;
- `refreshWsl` on the settings window's list();
- task binding (liveCommands → warm);
- apps.ts on a Linux-app launch;
- connections.ts for a `via: wsl` connect.

None of these runs while the user is just working in a terminal. So once a read has seen Ubuntu running, `running: true` lasts until one of these happens.

**Rig reproduction**
I copied the targets-runtime rig into /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/skeptic-wslnotice/test/unit/repro.test.ts. Setup: win32, WSL on with consent, Ubuntu `running: true` at the startup read, `runningNow()` returning an empty set, an ssh-looking terminal title, and the real `userSshProcessesWith` with a recording run(). Result:
- the noticer passed `{"wsl":{"exe":"C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe","distros":["Ubuntu"]}}`;
- the reader spawned the CIM PowerShell query and then `["C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe","-d","Ubuntu","--exec","/bin/sh","-s"]`;
- `wsl.facts` was called only once, at startup.

**Spec and residuals**
- design.md §2.7 says the WSL reader runs "only for running distros".
- §4.1 says nothing in discovery boots a VM.
- Critique wsl-20 (accepted) says a distro counts as stopped until an uncached `runningNow()` says otherwise, so that `wsl --terminate` is never undone. This path also undoes a user's `wsl --shutdown`.
- No L-item or handoffs.md residual covers it.

**Default gates do not block it**
`offerSsh` defaults to true. `cimAllowed` is true with no hosts and no dismissed offers. `WSL_SSH_PROVEN` only changes the wording of the offer, not the read.

**Severity**
"Major" is somewhat generous, but the finding stands. The harm is a distro (and possibly the VM) started without the user asking, again on each qualifying title change at least 10 s apart. That boot also runs the distro's systemd and boot command. It is not a data-safety or security breach. The precondition is narrower than "WSL is on": some read must have seen the distro running (Ember started while WSL was up, the settings window opened, a WSL task, a WSLg app). If Ember started before WSL, the flag stays false and the effect is a missed notice instead of a boot. The finding states this precondition correctly.

I couldn't refute this. The scenario holds from the WSL side.

1. **The reader trusts the cached flag.** In runtime.ts:943-947 the noticer's wsl() closure picks distros from `wslFacts.distros[].running` and the registry `entries`, and both come from the same cached facts. Nothing calls `wsl.runningNow()` or `isRunning()`. The notice-ssh.ts:316-321 reader then runs `execFile(wsl.exe, ["-d", d, "--exec", "/bin/sh", "-s"])`. That call starts a stopped distro, and it does not go through the job host or `WslRunner.runScript`. `runScript` re-checks `runningNow()` unless it is passed `mayBoot`, and `applyFix` (runtime.ts:1453-1455) does the same check before it acts.

2. **Nothing keeps the flag fresh.** `wslFacts` only changes through `wsl.onChange`, which fires from `publish` when `facts()` rediscovers, or from `applyRunning` via `runningNow` or `isRunning`'s background read. While Ember is idle, the only callers are these:
   - the router's `look()`: it returns before `facts()` when no RAIL (WSLg) window is on screen;
   - the router's 10 s `tick()`: it runs only while a WSLg helper sidecar exists (`ensureTicker`), and that helper stops once idle;
   - `refreshWsl`: at startup, when the settings window's Computers list loads (`TARGETS_IPC.list`, served from a 60 s cache), and when the user's words name WSL;
   - WSL runners: only during commands;
   - apps.ts: only on its first watch and when launching a WSLg app.

   No timer refreshes the running set. Once Ubuntu stops (idle timeout, or the user running `wsl --shutdown`), `running: true` stays until one of these happens.

3. **Nothing else blocks the read.** `offerSsh` defaults to true. `cimAllowed()` is true by default (no hosts and no dismissed offers). `wslOn()` only requires WSL to be on with consent, which the scenario assumes. The `listedOnly` filter comes from the same stale facts.

4. **Not an accepted residual.** No row in handoffs.md covers this, and neither do L1-L26. It contradicts design §2.7 ("The WSL reader runs only with WSL on, only for running distros"), §4.1/§4.2 (nothing boots a VM except work the user asked for there) and the WSL consent card's text (§8.4.1: "never starts a distro on its own").

5. **Reproduced.** I copied targets-runtime.test.ts into /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/sk2wsl/repro.test.ts with absolute imports and plugged the real `userSshProcessesWith` into a fake `run`. Startup read Ubuntu as running; I then made `runningNow()` return an empty set and `isRunning()` return false. One noticer tick on a "Windows Terminal" window titled "deploy@build-01: ~" made zero calls to `runningNow`, `isRunning` or `facts`. It passed `{wsl:{exe:"C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe",distros:["Ubuntu"]}}` and spawned `["C:\\Program Files\\WSL\\wsl.exe","-d","Ubuntu","--exec","/bin/sh","-s"]` after the CIM query. It repeats on every check, since a check reads processes before the per-key `offered` filter. The checks stop only once `cimAllowed()` turns false: the user dismisses an offer with no host saved.

**Severity:** "major" is defensible. The script itself is fixed and read-only, so nothing leaks. But Ember boots a VM and the distro's init (systemd services, if enabled) without being asked, and it can do so again on every check at least 10 s apart. That breaks a promise printed on the consent card.

**Small caveat:** opening the settings window after the 60 s facts cache has expired re-reads the running set. That fixes the flag only until the distro stops again, so it doesn't change the finding.

confirmed.title: GWSL's X server windows are not treated as remote surfaces, so Ember can act in them and they are not masked
confirmed.scenario: GWSL draws Linux apps through its bundled VcXsrv, whose program image is GWSL_vcxsrv.exe (or GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi.exe). The Windows backend names the window's app "GWSL_vcxsrv" (names.ts programName), and REMOTE_SURFACE.win32 / WINDOWS_X_SERVER only match the exact name `gwsl(.exe)`. The WSL doctor already expects this name: X_SERVERS uses /^gwsl.*\.exe$/ and reports "GWSL" for GWSL_vcxsrv.exe. Checked: isRemoteSurface("GWSL_vcxsrv","win32") is false, while "vcxsrv" is true. PolicyEngine.decide({kind:"keys", app:"GWSL_vcxsrv", window:"ana@pc: ~"}) returns confirm, where vcxsrv returns never. As a result, a Linux terminal, polkit or pinentry window shown by GWSL can be typed or clicked into through the borrowed keyboard and mouse after a single confirm. One grant on GWSL_vcxsrv covers every Linux app it shows, the same-process pointer check accepts any of its windows, and its windows are not blacked out in screenshots.
confirmed.fix: Match GWSL's real image names in both regexes, for example `gwsl(?:_vcxsrv(?:_lowdpi)?)?`, or reuse the doctor's gwsl.* rule, so REMOTE_SURFACE, isWindowsXServer and the doctor agree. Add a test for "GWSL_vcxsrv".

votes.reason:
I could not refute this. The scenario is real; only part of the stated impact is overstated.

What I checked:
1. GWSL's real X server binary. In GWSL's own source (Opticos/GWSL-Source manager.py), line 2784 launches `VCXSRV/GWSL_vcxsrv{hd}.exe`, and lines 1169-1170 and 4500-4501 name "GWSL_vcxsrv.exe" and "GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi.exe" as the X server processes. The only image that `gwsl(?:\.exe)?$` matches is GWSL.exe, the dashboard, which is an ordinary Windows window. So the `gwsl` entry in REMOTE_SURFACE.win32 (remote-surface.ts:31) and WINDOWS_X_SERVER (line 36) misses every Linux window GWSL shows.
2. How Ember names those windows. On Windows the app name is programName(processImage(pid)) (hwnd.ts:43, names.ts:23), so a GWSL window is "GWSL_vcxsrv" or "GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi". Policy only refuses remote surfaces through isRemoteSurface (policy.ts:2030), and Perception masks only windows whose wmClass passes the same check (perception/index.ts:676-679). I found no other guard: nothing checks window class and nothing else refers to X servers.
3. Running the code. I bundled the worktree code with esbuild and ran it from the scratchpad; the worktree was not touched. Results:
   - isRemoteSurface and isWindowsXServer are false for both GWSL_vcxsrv names, while runningXServer gives "GWSL" for both.
   - keys in "GWSL_vcxsrv" with window "ana@pc: ~" gives verdict confirm ("Borrow your keyboard to press A in GWSL_vcxsrv?"), with or without an act grant.
   - The same request in "vcxsrv" gives never, with REMOTE_SURFACE_REASON.
4. Specs. Design §4.6, L7 and critique wsl-15 explicitly require GWSL windows to be refused at every tier except read and open_app, and always masked. I found no accepted residual for this in handoffs.md or the L-list.
5. The doctor makes it worse. It detects GWSL (its rule `^gwsl.*\.exe$` matches GWSL_vcxsrv.exe and GWSL_service.exe) and tells the user "Linux apps shown by an X server ... can't be used", but Ember does act in them.

What is overstated:
- "After a single confirm" is wrong. Borrowed keyboard and mouse actions return everyTime:true and remember:false, and a grant does not skip the prompt, so every action asks the user and names GWSL_vcxsrv.
- "One grant covers every Linux app" mostly doesn't matter, because UI Automation sees nothing inside an X server window, so accessibility-tier actions have nothing to target.

What stands without any prompt:
- Screenshots never black out GWSL windows. That includes Linux apps the user put on the never-look list, and password prompts, which the never-look and password checks can't see into.
- Typing into a Linux terminal shown by GWSL goes out as a plain per-action confirm, without the terminal or security-window handling the design meant remote surfaces to get.

Severity: major is defensible. A safety and privacy boundary the design names explicitly does nothing for one of its five named X servers, and the masking failure is passive.

Fix: match `gwsl(?:_vcxsrv(?:_lowdpi)?)?` in both regexes. isWindowsXServer is only used in tests, so the policy and masking depend on the REMOTE_SURFACE change. Add tests for "GWSL_vcxsrv" and "GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi".

The scratch script is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/skeptic-gwsl/gwsl.ts.

I could not refute this. I confirmed the scenario in the code, by running it, and against GWSL's own source.

1. **GWSL's real program names.** GWSL starts its X server as `VCXSRV/GWSL_vcxsrv{hd}.exe`, where `hd` is "" or "_lowdpi" (Opticos/GWSL-Source manager.py:2781-2784; main.py:479-480 and 538). The Linux app windows therefore belong to GWSL_vcxsrv.exe or GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi.exe. GWSL.exe is only the dashboard, and GWSL_service.exe is the tray service. The doctor's own test already uses "GWSL_service.exe" (test/unit/wsl-discover.test.ts:477), so the doctor author knew GWSL's programs are named GWSL_*.

2. **What Ember calls the window.** `programName("...\\GWSL_vcxsrv.exe")` returns "GWSL_vcxsrv" (app/main/platform/win32/names.ts:23).

3. **No other check catches it.** `isRemoteSurface` is called in only two places: policy.ts:2030 and perception, through `remoteSurfaceCheck` (main.ts:1321). Both use the same `REMOTE_SURFACE.win32` regex, `^(?:...|gwsl)(?:\.exe)?$`. That regex matches only "gwsl" exactly. Nothing checks the window class or any other route. `isWindowsXServer` has no callers outside its own file and the tests, and its regex has the same gap.

4. **What a scratch vitest run against the worktree printed:**
   - `isRemoteSurface("GWSL_vcxsrv","win32")` is false, and so is "GWSL_vcxsrv_lowdpi".
   - `isRemoteSurface("vcxsrv","win32")` is true.
   - `isWindowsXServer("GWSL_vcxsrv")` is false.
   - `runningXServer(["GWSL_vcxsrv.exe"])` returns "GWSL", so the doctor and the policy disagree.
   - Policy for `keys` in "GWSL_vcxsrv" with window "ana@pc: ~": confirm/risky. The same request in "vcxsrv" is never/deny with REMOTE_SURFACE_REASON. A click in GWSL_vcxsrv gives "first action in GWSL_vcxsrv", needsGrant, remember:true. That is a grantable app, not a refusal.

5. **It is not an accepted residual.** handoffs.md has nothing about GWSL, X servers or remote surfaces. design.md L7 and §4.6 (critique wsl-15, "Accepted") say outright that Linux apps shown by GWSL are "refused and masked". This code is meant to do exactly that, and for GWSL it does not.

**Severity.** The strongest argument for downgrading is that this is no worse than the baseline at 832045e, because X servers were not remote surfaces at all before this diff. It is an incomplete fix, not a regression. Also, keystrokes still need a per-action confirm, and a polkit window titled "Authentication Required" would still be refused by the security-window title check.

I still don't think "major" is overstated:
- The design treats this as a safety rule (L7), and it fails for one of the five X servers it names.
- A single grant on GWSL_vcxsrv covers every Linux app GWSL shows.
- Those windows are not masked in screenshots.
- Terminal checks cannot see a Linux terminal inside them.
- The fix is easy: match `gwsl(?:_vcxsrv(?:_lowdpi)?)?`, or reuse the doctor's gwsl.* rule.

The scratch test is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/gwsl-test/gwsl.test.ts.

confirmed.title: A stale isRunning() permanently assigns a newly started distro's msrdc to another distro, so its Linux windows are never identified
confirmed.scenario: Ubuntu is running and Debian is stopped. The user asks "open gedit in Debian". launchWslg reads wsl.facts(), which is cached and does not refresh the running set, and then opens the .lnk; Debian boots and its msrdc (a new pid) shows gedit. The worker's first look() calls wsl.isRunning("Debian"), which returns the cached set (still stopped) and only starts a background refresh. So candidates=[Ubuntu] and showing=1, and line 327 maps Debian's msrdc pid to "Ubuntu". The mapping is only dropped when that msrdc exits or Ubuntu stops being a candidate, so it never corrects. Debian's windows are matched against Ubuntu's frames, no Debian helper is ever started, and the app Ember just opened stays "msrdc" (refused and masked) while Ubuntu runs. Reproduced with the router fakes: with isRunning("Debian") false on the first look and true on five later looks, the snapshot never contains hwnd 21 and helpers were created only for ["Ubuntu"]. In the control run, without the lag, 21 is identified as wsl:Debian:gedit.
confirmed.fix: Before using the single-running-distro shortcut, read the running set uncached (runningNow()), or don't cache an assignment made by that shortcut. Re-check pidDistro whenever the number of running WSL 2 distros grows.

votes.reason:
I could not refute this finding. I reproduced it, and "minor" is the right severity.

**Code path (router.ts at 06d2c29)**
- In service.ts, `isRunning` always returns the cached `running.set`. When the cache is more than 2 s old it starts `runningNow()` in the background, and it sets `runningInflight` synchronously.
- At lines 318/321 in router.ts, `isRunning` is called for every distro in the same synchronous filter pass. So in that look, `isRunning("Debian")` returns the stale false.
- `launchWslg` (apps.ts) only calls `wsl.facts()`. With the facts cache under 60 s old, that does not touch the running set. If it rediscovers, it records the running set from before the launch, when Debian was still stopped.
- **No Ubuntu windows on screen.** `look()` returns at line 308 before calling `isRunning`, there is no helper, and so no ticker. Nothing else polls (targets/runtime.ts calls `runningNow` only in `applyFix`). The first look that sees Debian's msrdc therefore always gets the stale answer, so this case is close to deterministic.
- **The mapping is never corrected.**
  - Line 327 maps the new msrdc pid to Ubuntu.
  - Line 323 keeps the mapping because Ubuntu is still a candidate.
  - The pid is no longer in `unresolved`, so `distroOfTitles` never runs for it, and Debian is never added to `consult`.
  - `factsChanged` only forgets distros that stopped.
  - `tick()` even keeps Ubuntu's helper from going idle, because it counts Debian's msrdc as Ubuntu's.

**Reproduction.** I wrote a scratch vitest using the repo's own fakes: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/sk1-wsl/lag.test.ts. In it, `isRunning("Debian")` is false on the first look only.
- With and without Ubuntu windows on screen, hwnd 21 is never identified over 6 looks, and helpers are created only for ["Ubuntu"].
- In the control run without the lag, 21 is `wsl:Debian:gedit` and a Debian helper is created.

**Not an accepted residual.** Nothing in handoffs.md, the lead notes or the L-list covers this. Design §4.9 says "one running distro → that one; cached per msrdc pid", which assumes the running set is accurate.

**Small overstatements, none of which refute it**
- The mapping is also dropped when that msrdc has no window left on screen (line 307 together with `WslgPids.of`), when the kill switch fires (`stopAll` forgets Ubuntu), or when WSL is turned off. So closing and reopening the app can fix it.
- A running Docker Desktop (a tool distro) makes the count of running distros 2, which disables the shortcut.

**Severity.** The result fails closed: the window is refused and masked, and no window is wrongly identified in this scenario. It is still a real, lasting failure to use the app Ember just opened, so "minor" is correct.

I couldn't refute this. I confirmed it in the code and reproduced it, and "minor" is the right severity.

1. **The cache is real.** `app/main/wsl/service.ts:184-189`: `isRunning()` returns the cached `running.set` (RUNNING_CACHE_MS = 2 s) and only starts a background `runningNow()`. `launchWslg` (`app/main/wsl/apps.ts:175`) calls `wsl.facts()`, which is cached for 60 s and does not refresh the running set after the boot. Nothing else refreshes it on a regular schedule. The runtime only calls `runningNow()` in the a11y fix, and the router ticker exists only while a helper is running.

2. **It is almost certain when Ubuntu has no Linux windows on screen.** `look()` returns early at `router.ts:308` when there are no RAIL windows, before it calls `isRunning`. So no look refreshes the running set while Debian boots. The first look that sees Debian's msrdc reads a running set taken before the boot. When Ubuntu does have RAIL windows, it is a narrower race: the cache is about 2-4 s old against Debian's WSLg start-up time.

3. **The mapping is never corrected while the window stays open.** At line 327, `candidates=[Ubuntu]` and `showing=1`, so Debian's pid is mapped to Ubuntu. On later looks Debian is a candidate, but line 323 only drops mappings whose distro is no longer a candidate, and Ubuntu still is. Line 326 excludes pids that already have a mapping from `unresolved`, so `consult` stays {Ubuntu} and Debian is never asked. `factsChanged` only forgets distros that stopped, and `start()`'s uncached `runningNow()` runs after the mapping is already made. `tick()` even keeps Ubuntu's helper from going idle, because Debian's pid is mapped to Ubuntu.

4. **Reproduced.** Scratch test: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/skeptic-wsl-lag/lag.test.ts, using the real `wsl-fakes` harness and `router.ts`. In it, `isRunning("Debian")` is false on the first look only, then true for 5 more looks. hwnd 21 is never identified and helpers are created only for ["Ubuntu"], both with and without an Ubuntu window on screen. In the control run without the lag, 21 is identified as `wsl:Debian:gedit` and helpers are created for Ubuntu and Debian.

5. **Not covered by any accepted residual.** Nothing in handoffs.md, the design's L-list or the decisions covers this. Design §4.9 says "one running distro with WSLg → that one; … cached per msrdc pid until it exits", and the router's own header promises that running checks are uncached before they are relied on.

6. **Small overstatement.** "Permanently" is not quite right. The mapping is also dropped when Debian's msrdc has no window left in the stack (line 307), and on the kill switch, WSL off, or Ubuntu stopping. It does persist for as long as the app Ember just opened stays on screen.

**Severity.** Minor is right. The failure is fail-closed: the window stays "msrdc", refused and masked, so the app Ember opened can't be used. That is a functional bug, not a safety one. A cross-distro wrong match would need an Ubuntu frame with the same title. WSLg's " (Debian)" title suffix, which `railTitle` strips only for the distro being matched, makes that unlikely.

confirmed.title: A WSLg shortcut whose Linux command starts with VAR=value passes the terminal check, so Ember opens a terminal
confirmed.scenario: The shortcut is `wslg.exe -d Ubuntu --cd "~" -- GDK_BACKEND=x11 gnome-terminal`. Such a shortcut can come from a user-writable .desktop file in the distro, which is the threat critique wsl-23 names. TOKEN allows '=', so wslgLaunch accepts argv ["GDK_BACKEND=x11","gnome-terminal"]. The distro's shell reads the first word as an assignment and starts gnome-terminal. linuxTerminal() calls isTerminalApp({argv}, "linux"), which treats "gdk_backend=x11" as the program, so the answer is not a terminal (the same command written with `env` is detected). Verified: isTerminalApp returned false, and launch() spawned explorer.exe with the .lnk. The same check is at line 180 in launchWslg. Ember opens a terminal (or `X=1 bash`), breaking 'Ember never opens terminals'.
confirmed.fix: Judge the Linux command as the shell will run it: skip leading NAME=value words (for example call linuxTerminal with ["env", ...p.argv]), or reject an assignment word in command position in wslgLaunch.

votes.reason:
I could not refute it. The bug is real in the code, though its practical effect is smaller than the write-up suggests.

What I confirmed: I bundled app/main/wsl/apps.ts with esbuild and ran it against fake files, spawn and WSL facts, using the fixture shape from test/unit/wsl-apps.test.ts. The scratch script is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Ember-Powered-by-Github-Copilot/9df81ff3-d6fa-5078-ac02-9c8dbaa6cb03/scratchpad/sk1-wslg/repro.ts. These tails:
- `GDK_BACKEND=x11 gnome-terminal`
- `A=b xterm`
- `X=1 bash`

all pass `wslgLaunch` (TOKEN allows '='). For each, `isTerminalApp` returns false and `launch()` spawns `explorer.exe` with the .lnk. The same command written with `env` in front is refused. The cause is in `runsTerminal`: it skips NAME=VALUE words only inside `envCommand`, so a bare assignment is taken as the program name. Design §4.8 and critique wsl-23 both say that after `--`, wslg hands the tail to the distro's default shell, so the shell would treat the word as an assignment.

Nothing guards against this elsewhere. It is not one of the accepted residuals in handoffs.md, and no limitation in L1-L26 covers it. The design lists '=' in the allowed token characters but never mentions assignment words in command position.

Why the severity is lower than the write-up suggests (minor at most, close to hardening):
1. It adds nothing for the attacker critique wsl-23 assumes, a distro process that writes a .desktop file. These tails also pass by design and also start whatever the attacker wants:
   - `sh /home/ana/.cache/calc`
   - `/home/ana/.local/bin/calc`
   - `python3 /home/ana/x.py`

   I ran all three: each launched. The reason is in `runsTerminal`, which says "A script runs: refuse only a script that is itself a terminal". Limitation L8 already accepts that what a script does inside isn't judged. The same attacker can also start gnome-terminal directly from inside the distro.
2. Ember still can't use the terminal once it is open:
   - An identified `wsl:<distro>:gnome-terminal-server` window is refused through `wslAwarePrivacy`'s Linux terminal names (privacy.ts:62-67, including the 15-character truncation rule).
   - Mouse and keyboard actions (tier 3) are refused in every WSLg window (L7, target-rules.ts).
   - An unidentified window such as xterm stays "msrdc", a remote surface refused at every tier.

   So the core of the "never opens terminals" rule, that Ember never types into a terminal, still holds. Only the letter of "never opens one" is broken.

confirmed.title: Apps of a running root distro are launched because the root check only uses a uid learned from commands
confirmed.scenario: Example: an imported distro whose default user is root is running, and no Ember command has run there yet. WslDistro.defaultUid is filled only by learnedUid() from a command runner's facts. The router learns uid 0 from the helper's status, but only sets st.problem="root" and does not feed the uid back into the facts. So facts.defaultUid is null and wslgRefusal returns null. launchWslg never asks WslService.defaultUid(), which exists to read the uid of a running distro without booting it. Verified with a fake service whose defaultUid("Ubuntu") resolves 0 and whose facts have defaultUid:null and running:true: launch() spawned explorer.exe with the gedit .lnk. §4.8 says a root default user is rejected, and L17 says WSLg apps of a root distro stay refused; here Ember starts the GUI app as root.
confirmed.fix: In launchWslg, when the target distro is running and defaultUid is null, await wsl.defaultUid(distro) (it never boots) and refuse on 0. Alternatively, have the router record a helper's uid 0 in the service's uid map.

confirmed.scenario: The PC runs Windows. WSL is not installed, or it is installed but the user never turned it on in Ember (or an admin policy sets features.wsl:false). Commands are off and there is no SSH host. The user says "Open Edge and search for how to install Python on Linux" or "Show me how to open a PDF in WSL". 1) It is the specified, deliberate design. The handoffs.md WRONG-TARGET fix (DOC's review) has two separate requirements. One is that D4.4 never announces. Commit dd672bb lists "a Host of the user's ssh config" as a computer the user named, and says "the task's bubbles say where it runs, this computer included". Design §2.4 says "The user must always know where an action will happen", and T23 (wrong target) applies to "all" kinds and is mitigated by "the target badge everywhere". GUI tasks are also exposed to the wrong target. Example: commands off, ~/.ssh/config has `Host work`, Ember has no record of it, and the user says "work: close all my windows". bind() matches only Ember's own entries, so the task binds to this computer and closes local windows. No action, question, announcement or result changes. The only residual is a cosmetic extra truthful label when a word happens to match an alias (such as "github.com" or "pi"). That is a nit the design chose to accept, leaning towards showing more rather than less, not a minor bug.
